title: Job 25:1–6
context: Bildad the Shuhite speaks for the third and last time (25:1). His speech is only six verses long, the shortest of the friends’ speeches, and after it no third speech from Zophar appears in the book as it stands. Bildad praises God’s dominion and the vastness of his armies (25:2–3), then asks how a man can be just with God or how one born of a woman can be clean (25:4), arguing from the lesser brightness of moon and stars to the lowliness of man, “who is a worm” (25:5–6). His question echoes Job’s own (9:2) and Eliphaz’s (4:17; 15:14–16), but here it serves to silence Job’s claim of integrity. This is a friend’s speech, not the book’s last word on righteousness: the reader knows from 1:8 and 2:3 that God calls Job blameless, and the LORD later says the friends have not spoken of him what is right (42:7). Many readers hear the brevity of the speech as a sign that the friends’ case is running out of words; some also propose that part of chapter 26 continues Bildad’s speech, a view noted with 26:5–14 and left open here.

verses.arminianNotes: The narrator introduces Bildad the Shuhite for his third speech, answering Job’s complaint in chapters 23–24 that God seems absent and the wicked go unpunished. Arminian readers note that Bildad does not engage Job’s specific questions, and they hear in his reply a theology that defends God’s majesty while overlooking the sufferer in front of him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Bildad returning to the friends’ framework rather than to Job’s actual complaint, and they note that orthodox-sounding speech can still be misapplied. Shared ground: both traditions read what follows as Bildad’s case, reported faithfully by the book, but not adopted by it as its own verdict on Job.

verses.text: “Dominion and fear are with him. He makes peace in his high places.
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad opens with God’s dominion and fear, and says he “makes peace in his high places.” Some readers hear an allusion to conflict in the heavens that God subdues, though the image is debated. Arminian readers affirm the truth of God’s sovereign majesty, while noting that Bildad uses it to close the conversation rather than to comfort Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers welcome the confession that dominion belongs to God and that he establishes order even in the heights, a theme the LORD himself develops in chapters 38–41. Shared ground: both traditions agree that the statement about God is true in itself; the question the book raises is whether Bildad applies it rightly to Job.

verses.text: Can his armies be counted? On whom does his light not arise?
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad asks whether God’s armies can be counted and on whom his light does not arise. Many readers take the armies as heavenly hosts or the stars (compare Isaiah 40:26). Arminian readers hear a genuine affirmation that God’s light reaches all people, a theme they connect with God’s universal care and kindness toward everyone he has made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in the countless armies a picture of God’s vast, ordered rule over all creatures, and in the light that arises on everyone a reminder of common grace (compare Matthew 5:45). Shared ground: both traditions agree that God’s power and goodness reach everywhere, and both note that Bildad stops short of applying that goodness to Job.

verses.text: How then can man be just with God? Or how can he who is born of a woman be clean?
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad asks how man can be just with God, or how one born of a woman can be clean, a question Job himself raised (9:2) and Eliphaz pressed (4:17; 15:14). Arminian readers affirm that all people stand in need of God’s grace, yet note that Bildad uses the truth to deny Job’s integrity, which God himself affirmed (1:8; 2:3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in the question a real truth about human sinfulness before a holy God, one that the rest of Scripture develops (compare Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:23). Yet they caution against treating Bildad as the book’s teacher on justification. Shared ground: both traditions affirm the need for grace while rejecting Bildad’s use of the point against Job.

verses.text: Behold, even the moon has no brightness, and the stars are not pure in his sight;
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad argues that even the moon has no brightness and the stars are not pure in God’s sight. Arminian readers take this as poetic hyperbole meant to show the gulf between Creator and creation, and they note that elsewhere the heavens declare God’s glory (Psalm 19:1) rather than standing under reproach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a heightened contrast between God’s holiness and the brightest created things, similar to Eliphaz’s claim that the heavens are not clean in his sight (15:15). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry about God’s incomparable holiness, not as a claim that the moon and stars are morally guilty.

verses.text: How much less man, who is a worm, and the son of man, who is a worm!”
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad closes by calling man a worm and the son of man a worm, ending his speech abruptly. Arminian readers note that Scripture can use such language for human frailty (compare Psalm 22:6), yet they set it beside Psalm 8:4–5, where God crowns humanity with glory, and they see Bildad’s picture as partial and unkind to Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm human lowliness before God and the depth of human need, but they also note that Bildad offers no word of mercy or redemption, unlike Job’s own hope of a redeemer (19:25). Shared ground: both traditions hold that humans are frail and dependent, and both decline to treat Bildad’s bleak closing line as the book’s last word on humanity.
